newsitem.title: THAILAND: Anson Chan says freedom key to Hong Kong success.
newsitem.headline: Anson Chan says freedom key to Hong Kong success.

text.p: Top Hong Kong civil servant Anson Chan said on Tuesday that press freedom and free flows of information were essential to the success of post-handover Hong Kong.

"Press freedom and ensuring free flows of information are crucial to Hong Kong's success, 80 percent of Hong Kong's gross domestic product comes from services, and those services are based on knowledge," she told a business meeting in Bangkok.
After more than 150 years of British rule, the colony reverts to China on July 1, and critics remain concerned that Beijing will curb press freedom in Hong Kong.

Chan, who is current governor Chris Patten's deputy, told an audience of leading businessmen that she understood the concerns of Hong Kong citizens who wished to have an elected assembly, independent judiciary, and free press following the handover.

"We believe that vigorous public discussion, both in media and in the Legislative Council, is the most effective way of ensuring that the government's financial proposals, like its legislature and policy proposals, are thoroughly tested for their economic good sense and their contribution to the well-being of the community," she added.
Under terms of the handover agreement, China has promised to run Hong Kong as a Special Administrative Region with a high degree of autonomy for 50 years.
Chan said there were several persuasive arguments to suggest that pledges made by China in a 1984 Sino-British agreement guaranteeing freedom of the press and democratic elections would be honoured.

"The building blocks are in place for a high degree of autonomy with the one country, two systems concept, and that it will be up to the people of Hong Kong themselves to determine the shape of the future," Chan said.
Chan, whose family comes from Shanghai, has elected to stay in Hong Kong after the handover where she will perform a similar role for Hong Kong's first post colonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa.
She said problems remained between China and Britain defining permanent residence qualifications and freedom of travel for Hong Kong's more than six million residents.
"We are very close to hammering out remaining details of this package...," she said.
Chan is due to discuss handover details with Tung and Chinese Premier Li Peng in the Chinese capital Beijing later this week.
"I will try to reflect Hong Kong peoples' views... I'm sure the Chinese leaders will be hospitable," she told Reuters.
